lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.title: Independent application A: measures of center

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: One reference example. Use it only if you get stuck.

items.prompt: A sample of 5 values is: 12, 15, 18, 20, 25. What is the mean of this data set?

steps: Divide by the number of values: 90 ÷ 5 = 18.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A data set has 5 values: 30, 32, 26, 22, 27. What is the new mean if an outlier of 54 is added to the data set, making 6 values in all?
A data set is: 24, 9, 17, 9, 21, with a mean of 16. What is the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of this data set?
Two data sets have means of 40 and 53. Their mean absolute deviation (MAD) is 8. Express the difference between the means as a multiple of the MAD.
choices: 1 5/8 times the MAD
5/8 times the MAD
13 times the MAD
8 times the MAD

items.prompt: Sample A: 22, 39, 24, 39, 26, 12. Sample B: 42, 37, 26, 39, 40, 50. Based on the means, which sample tends to have greater values?
choices: Sample A, with a mean of 27 compared to 39.
Both samples have the same mean.
Sample B, with a mean of 39 compared to 27.
Sample B, with a mean of 27 compared to 39.

items.prompt: Sample A: 53, 57, 55, 58, 56, 53. Sample B: 52, 57, 37, 65, 75, 71. Based on the range of each sample, which sample is more consistent (less variable)?
choices: Sample A, with a range of 38 compared to 5.
Sample B, with a range of 38 compared to 5.
Sample A, with a range of 5 compared to 38.
Both samples have the same range.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to know about all 985 visitors to a science museum. She randomly selects 246 of them to survey. What is the sample in this situation?
choices: All 985 visitors to a science museum
Only the first 246 visitors to a science museum on a list
The 246 randomly selected visitors to a science museum
The researcher's own estimate

items.prompt: A student posts an online form, and 59 commuters on a train line choose to respond. Is this sampling method likely to produce a representative sample?
choices: No, likely not representative — the method favors certain members over others.
Yes, likely representative, because the sample size is large enough.
Yes, likely representative — every member had a fair, known chance of being chosen.
No, likely not representative, because the population is too large.

items.prompt: In a random sample of 29 commuters on a train line, 19 preferred a new park design. Based on this sample, about how many of the 203 commuters on a train line would you expect to prefer a new park design?

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Mastery check. Work without help, then stop and hand this section in.

items.prompt: Five random samples of the same population produced these mean scores: 19, 28, 24, 19, 28. What is the range of these sample estimates?

A population has 1030 shoppers at a grocery store. Student A takes a random sample of 31. Student B takes a random sample of 14. Both use proper random selection. Whose sample is more likely to give an estimate closer to the true population value?
choices: Student A's sample of 31, because larger random samples tend to produce more consistent, accurate estimates.
Neither sample is reliable unless it includes the entire population.
Both are equally likely to be accurate, because both are random.
Student B's sample of 14, because smaller samples are easier to analyze.

items.prompt: A student surveys 68 commuters on a train line using a convenience sample of her classmates only and records the results. Is it valid to generalize this result to all 1836 commuters on a train line?
choices: No, because samples can never be generalized to a population.
Yes, because the sample was selected randomly, so it is likely representative of the population.
No, because the sample was not randomly selected, so it may not represent the population.
Yes, because the sample size is large enough regardless of how it was chosen.
